newsitem.title: JAPAN: New blow to US military in Japan sex assault case.
newsitem.headline: New blow to US military in Japan sex assault case.

text.p: An American sailor was under arrest at the main U.S. naval base in Japan on Thursday on suspicion of beating and sexually assaulting his Japanese girlfriend in his quarters.

The incident threatens to be a new blow to the image of the U.S. military both at home and abroad. A police spokesman said it occurred at Yokosuka Naval Base on the outskirts of Tokyo during an argument between the pair.

No formal charges had yet been filed over Wednesday's incident, which could cause new tension in U.S.-Japan relations after the widely publicised 1995 gang rape of a Japanese schoolgirl on Okinawa by three U.S. servicemen.

The case could not have come at a worse time both for Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who is battling to ensure the future of U.S. military bases here, and U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen, who makes his first visit to Japan next week.
Police said the 21-year-old woman had told them the couple had dated for about eight months and her injuries happened during a drunken quarrel at about 3 a.m. over a "small thing".
Yokosuka deputy police chief Satoshi Nakajima told Reuters the woman said her 27-year-old boyfriend grabbed her during the argument and then dropped her on a bed.
She bounced off the bed and fell on the floor, breaking her collarbone, he quoted her as saying.
"Apparently, this is not a case of rape," Nakajima said. "The results of the medical examination of the victim show no evidence of rape."
Police were treating the case as one of assault only.

In a bid to head off criticism that followed the Okinawa rape case, U.S. military authorities notified Japanese police of the incident within an hour and also allowed police to almost immediately question the suspect.
In the Okinawa case, there were complaints that the U.S. military did not fully cooperate with local police.
Under new legal arrangements worked out since the Okinawa incident, Japanese police have full jurisdiction in the case.
But naval officials said even if police did not decide to prosecute the sailor, the military authorities could take their own action if they felt a case still existed under U.S. law.
A U.S. Navy statement said the petty officer third class was in custody after Yokosuka Base security forces responded to a disturbance at the bachelor's enlisted quarters.

"Upon arrival, they found a 21-year-old Japanese woman who had been beaten and allegedly sexually assaulted by an E-4 (third class petty officer) assigned to Yokosuka Naval Computer and Telecommunications Station," the statement said.
The woman was treated at the base hospital for a broken clavicle, abrasions and bruises to the arms, legs and neck.
"Navy policy demands the highest standards of behaviour...at all times, wherever they (Navy personnel) are, and views with gravest concern any incidents of misconduct," the statement added.

The case became public on the day that Hashimoto submitted a bill to parliament that would forcibly extend leases on some privately owned land occupied by the bases on Okinawa, home to more than half of the 47,000 U.S. troops in Japan.
The Okinawa rape case, for which three U.S. servicemen are serving jail terms, set off a campaign by local authorities which want the bases closed by 2015.
At stake are plots of land owned by 3,000 anti-bases activists who are refusing to renew the contracts. Another 29,000 landowners have agreed to renew their leases.
